observations.observed: The landing zone schedules agent updates for Saturday 02:00 in each host's local time, one window, while its scaling plan can leave a pooled pool with no running host overnight and at weekends (the weekend schedule's minimum is 0%) and its optional auto shutdown deallocates hosts at night; nothing starts hosts for the window. On a pool with no host running at 02:00 the scheduled update can't run, and after four missed windows the broker installs it by force at a time nobody chose. The schedule needs a second window inside hours when hosts are on, or a step that starts the hosts for the window. Read from the code, not yet seen in a run.

An alerting model needs someone to receive the alerts, not only alert rules. The landing zone creates its six log alerts (unhealthy hosts, FSLogix errors, connection errors, low disk, low memory, high CPU) on every deployment, enabled, but attaches an action group only when alert addresses are given; without them the rules fire with nobody notified, and the Service Health alert isn't created at all. An assessment that counts alert rules alone would score that estate as alerted, so the alert fact counts rules with and without an action group separately (gap:monitoring-scope). The landing zone also has no Azure Files metric alert (throttling or capacity, review checklist E02.03); its FSLogix alert reads host event logs only.

Budgets only alert, so the landing zone wires its budget to an action group that runs a Lock runbook, and avd-swarm's spend guard enforces caps before a lab run opens instead of relying on the budget. For AVD a plain deallocate isn't enough either, because Start VM on Connect and the scaling plan start the hosts again at the next sign-in or ramp-up; Lock drains, sets the scaling plan exclusion tag and turns Start VM on Connect off. The budget-to-runbook path hasn't run against a real deployment yet.

The landing zone's image build brings Microsoft Defender Antivirus signatures up to date and fails the build if they stay older than a day, but it doesn't run the cache maintenance task before the image is sealed, which the source says avoids higher CPU on each new host while the task runs. How much CPU and logon time that costs on the first sessions of a new host is unmeasured (gap:security-agents-scope).

Deleting the landing zone's demo hosts left their Entra ID and Intune device records behind until the cleanup script deleted them through Graph; a cleanup whose Graph sign-in timed out couldn't find the names on a second run until the fix kept the deployment record. Anything that recreates hosts (session host update, a rebuild) leaves the same records unless a step removes them.

The landing zone turns encryption at host on by default and registers the subscription feature it needs, so it never uses Azure Disk Encryption. No run has measured whether it changes host performance, which the source says it doesn't.

avd-current-state's validator probes a fixed list of AVD endpoints from wherever it runs, usually Cloud Shell, and says so; that proves nothing about the session host subnet. Its list also predates the current required list (newer service domains, the relay UDP range, certificate endpoints on TCP 80, the platform addresses). An authoritative result needs the Agent URL Tool's output from a host, and a probe off the host should count as unknown, not pass.

The landing zone prices the compiled plan from retail prices before anything is deployed, with run hours from the power settings and an upper bound where the schedule rather than use decides (168 hours a week without a scheduled stop). Lab runs in the family don't start without that written estimate, a cap and teardown evidence, and avd-swarm's spend guard refuses a run whose estimate has an unpriced line or passes a cap. Retail prices are list prices, so the estimate is an upper bound for anyone with negotiated rates or commitments.

The landing zone keeps storage account key access off on its profile account for the default snapshot-tier backup and turns it on only for the vaulted tier, because two Microsoft pages differ: the support matrix asks for key access, the portal guide accepts key access off when public network access is disabled (ref:files-backup-portal#keys-or-private), which the landing zone does (its recovery spec, facts F14 and F19, open question U1). No real backup job has run with keys off, so whether the default profile backup works at all is unproven. The first landing zone run that reads the last backup job answers it; until then a reviewer treats a key-access-off share with a snapshot policy as unknown, not as backed up.

The landing zone applies the published FSLogix file and process exclusions to Microsoft Defender Antivirus on every host and doesn't fail the host when tamper protection or an endpoint policy owns exclusions, which means an assessment has to read the effective exclusions on the host rather than trust the deployment.

The landing zone loads FSLogix profiles from Azure Files with Entra Kerberos for cloud-only users on Entra joined hosts, with no AD DS and no synced accounts, once the share allowed AES-128-GCM. The prerequisites page and the Entra joined hosts page (ref:avd-entra-joined-hosts#fslogix-hybrid-users) still say hybrid accounts are needed, while the Azure Files and FSLogix pages support cloud-only identities (ref:files-entra-kerberos#cloud-only-and-hybrid, ref:fslogix-entra-profile#cloud-only-supported). The method follows the newer pages and treats cloud-only users as supported in the Azure public cloud.

The landing zone's host configuration sets part of the published list, in Microsoft Defender Antivirus's local preferences only: the temporary and share VHD and VHDX files and three FSLogix processes, one no longer on the list. Folders, Cloud Cache, drivers, registry keys and mount points aren't set; a third-party antivirus or a network or data loss prevention layer gets nothing; a central policy that owns exclusions only draws a warning. Logon impact untested.

The landing zone writes the Standard example on every host (one VHD location, VHDX, no ODFC, ProfileType unset, no redirections.xml, the recommended retry and local-profile values) and adds PreventLoginWithFailure and PreventLoginWithTempProfile, so a user whose container fails to attach can't sign in to a temporary profile and lose work silently. Its readiness script reads only Enabled and VHDLocations back on the host; no family tool reads the rest.

In hub-peered mode the landing zone routes 0.0.0.0/0 from the host subnet to the hub firewall and adds no route for the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag to the internet, the bypass the source gives against disconnections during firewall scale-in. With AVD Private Link on, the session host's gateway connection goes through the private endpoint, which may cover the main path; other service traffic still crosses the firewall. Not yet run against a hub firewall.

The landing zone enrolls its Entra joined hosts in Intune by default (the Entra login extension carries Intune's MDM ID) but assigns no configuration, compliance, baseline or update policy; its scope page leaves those to the organization. An enrolled host is therefore not yet a managed one, and under the tenant's default compliance setting it counts as compliant with no policy at all. Enrollment and policy are separate rows for that reason.

The landing zone sends every diagnostic category of its host pool, application group and workspace to its workspace and ships three log alerts a triage can start from - more than 10 admin-fixable errors (ServiceError false) by code in the window, a host whose latest agent health row is neither Available nor Upgrading (with no power-state filter, so a host that reported Unavailable just before it was deallocated can fire it), and any FSLogix error event. The split by ServiceError follows the source; the threshold of 10 and the Upgrading exclusion are the family's own choices, not published numbers, and no run has yet checked that the alerts fire on a broken host.

The landing zone builds the proof of concept's shape. Its sizing keeps a list of host pools but allows one entry today, sized from one workload's users per vCPU, so every user is one persona until a use case assessment says otherwise.

Microsoft's pages disagree on the scope autoscale's power role needs. The scaling plan page says anything below the subscription stops autoscale working; the autoscale troubleshooting page accepts the host pool, its resource group or the subscription (ref:troubleshoot-autoscale#role-scope-containing-pool). The landing zone assigns the role on its control plane and session host resource groups only. avd-landing-zone tracks the test as its issue 101. No run has yet read the autoscale diagnostics to show whether that works; if it does, this becomes a disagrees verdict for the brain's upstream list.

The landing zone's session hosts use Premium SSD OS disks, as the source recommends for production. No run has compared disk latency on Standard SSD or an ephemeral OS disk, so the choice rests on the source, not our evidence.

The landing zone enforces an NSG on its private endpoint subnet that allows TCP 445 from the hosts and TCP 443 from the network and denies the rest, while the source says the connection endpoint needs TCP 1-65535 whenever ports to it are restricted. Recorded sandbox runs connected sessions through landing zones built this way (to confirm from their run records), so either the session host side only needs 443 or the gap shows up under conditions not yet run (private client connections, other gateways). To test in a run that already deploys the landing zone, then record agrees or disagrees.

The landing zone uses the connection-only layout: one connection endpoint per host pool, host pool public access enabled for clients with session hosts private, the workspace feed public and no global endpoint. Users connect from any network while hosts reach the service privately, which is a layout the source supports; users who must also connect privately need the feed and global endpoints and client-side DNS, which the landing zone doesn't build.

The landing zone's same-tenant recovery design (recovery spec, scope and section 4) chooses a tier per landing zone, R0 rebuild, R1 restore anywhere or R2 warm standby (active-passive), and takes its RTO and RPO from Microsoft's estimates; active-active is a non-goal there. Its status check, configuration snapshot and profile recovery test are built and tested offline only: no recovery test has run against a real tenant, so none of the tier targets is measured. The first profile recovery test needs a written estimate and the owner's go; its run record (C17, use case recovery) becomes the evidence that turns this into agrees or disagrees.

The landing zone's default RDP properties turn drive, USB and COM port redirection off but keep clipboard, printers, smart cards, WebAuthn and the camera, because users need them. Restricting redirection is a per-property trade-off, so the method reports each one kept on as a warn with its reason, not as a gap.
Latency measured from Cloud Shell says nothing about users, because Cloud Shell runs in an Azure datacenter. Measure round-trip time from the user's device, against endpoints verified to be regional.

A real preflight run priced session hosts and OS disks as unmatched because the API returned lookalike meters with the same SKU and meter name, a CloudServices product at the Windows rate beside Virtual Machines at the base rate, and a Premium Page Blob meter beside Premium SSD Managed Disks. Private Link and NAT Gateway are listed only under the Global region. A price is matched on product, SKU and meter, and a line that matches none or several is reported with what it saw rather than guessed.

The run recorder spec keeps each run's expected and actual cost as contract C17 (avd-run-cost/v1), appends a reading until it is unchanged for 72 hours, and reports pending rather than a guess until then. For scale, an earlier one-host sandbox demo cost 0.97 USD for about eight hours. How long the actual took to appear in a pay-as-you-go sandbox hasn't been measured yet (the spec's open question U5).

The landing zone deploys a power management scaling plan (depth-first ramp-down that stops hosts at zero sessions, without forcing sign-out) and Start VM on Connect on by default, and every resource group and resource carries workload and environment tags. No run has yet compared a month of running hours with the schedule, so the saving is Microsoft's claim, not our evidence. The landing zone doesn't set the cm-resource-parent tag.

The landing zone's minimum kit defaults to a 4-vCPU memory-optimized host, which is Microsoft's stated floor and below its 6 to 24 vCPU range, chosen for the smallest test cost. The reasoning that shared hosts run out of memory before CPU is our hypothesis; no measurement backs it yet.

Hardening the profile share to AES-256-GCM as the only SMB channel encryption denied every Entra Kerberos session; allowing AES-128-GCM as well, with CCM still off, let users in. Encryption in transit stays on, but the strictest setting isn't usable with Entra Kerberos, so the method treats AES-128-GCM plus AES-256-GCM as passing.

Both landing zone network modes give hosts symmetric NAT egress, a NAT Gateway when standalone and the hub firewall when hub-peered, so by Microsoft's claim public-network Shortpath should relay through TURN, never connect directly. TURN itself needs outbound UDP 3478 to the relay range; where the egress firewall doesn't allow it, sessions fall back to TCP instead. How much round-trip time the relay adds is unmeasured.

Two Learn pages query a WVDConnections UdpUse column, while the table reference lists TransportType (Shortpath, TURN, Websocket) and no UdpUse, and Insights uses a third set of values. The family's connection query reads TransportType but hasn't run against a real workspace yet; one sandbox connection settles which column exists. Until then the method maps all three (gap:transport-classification).
The landing zone deploys every session host with Trusted launch, Secure Boot and vTPM on, from Gen2 images, and the demo host pool ran on it with no boot or image problem.

The landing zone sets size, host count and session limit as parameters, but fixes breadth-first load balancing and the scaling plan's capacity thresholds and minimum host shares (60% and 20% at ramp-up, 90% and 10% at ramp-down) in its control plane module, and lists the schedule as set by hand. A tuning loop can change the first three through the landing zone; the scaling levers it can only record until they become parameters.

Adopted as the landing zone's automatic sizing input, and its preflight warns above 6 sessions per vCPU. No real users have been measured against it, so the numbers are still Microsoft's prior, not our evidence.
The landing zone's image build keeps WDOT's Appx package removal off for this reason; no sysprep failure has been seen with it off. Not yet tested with it on.

WDOT's DiskCleanup category deletes every log, trace and event log file on the system drive, including an image build's own evidence before the image test reads it. The landing zone keeps that category off and cleans narrowly instead.

What runs inside the guest isn't visible from the control plane, but the landing zone's image build tags each gallery image version with the WDOT release, commit and profile hash it ran, so a Reader can see which pin and profile an image claims. Images built any other way carry no such record.

The landing zone spreads session hosts across zones 1, 2 and 3 by default (availabilityZones; an empty list deploys them regional) and keeps its profile share on zone-redundant storage, which follows the source. It doesn't add hosts for a lost zone: the host count is the operator's, so the n-1 headroom the source asks for is a sizing decision left to compute.host-count, and a two-host pool loses half its capacity with one zone.
